column2: This alone is the end of all, whatever is and is not; for one who knows its end, middle, being and non-being.
Total renunciation, "peace," "contentment": so it is settled; the good here is established in liberation.
The right, the true, the known and the knowable, the self of all, the moving and the unmoving, all happiness, the auspicious and the highest, Brahman, the unmanifest, the origin and the imperishable:
radiance, forbearance, peace, freedom from disease, the auspicious, space likewise eternal and firm: it is reached by these words with the eyes of intellect; honour to that Brahman, to the brahmana."
[Bhishma said:] "Here I shall relate to you an ancient tale of how Kundadhara long ago, out of affection, helped a devotee.
A certain poor brahmana, from desire, looked to dharma; wishing wealth for sacrifice, he performed dreadful austerity.
Having made his resolve, he worshipped the deities with devotion, but did not gain wealth by worshipping the deities.
Then he fell into worry again: "Which deity is it that would quickly be gracious to me, not made dull by men?"
Then, near him, he saw with a gentle form an attendant of the gods, a cloud-bearer, Kundadhara, standing.
On seeing that great soul, devotion arose in him: "He will give me good fortune, for his form is such.
He is near the god and not surrounded by other men; he will give me abundant wealth, and quickly."
Then the twice-born worshipped him with incense, perfumes, garlands of various kinds, and many kinds of offerings.
Then the brahmana, by the radiance of Kundadhara, saw in a dream all beings, lying on kusha grass.
The brahmana, pure of self, unadorned, through calm, austerity and devotion, saw an example in the night.
He saw Manibhadra there, of great radiance, the great-souled one among the gods, giving orders, Yudhishthira.
There the gods give kingdoms and wealth; those engaged in good deeds cut off the evil ones.
Then, while the yakshas watched, Kundadhara of great radiance, coming out, fell on the ground before the gods, bull of the Bharatas.
Then, by the gods' word, Manibhadra of great fame said to him fallen on the ground: "Kundadhara, what is wished?"
[Kundadhara said:] "If the gods are pleased with me, this brahmana is my devotee; I wish to do him a favour that brings happiness."
[Bhishma said:] Then Manibhadra spoke again to Kundadhara of great radiance, by the word of the gods:
Rise, rise, good luck to you; your work done, be happy. As much wealth as this friend of yours the brahmana wishes, by the command of the gods I give an immeasurable amount.
But Kundadhara, reflecting that human life is unsteady and impermanent, set his mind on the austerity of that famous brahmana.
[Kundadhara said:] "I do not ask for wealth for the brahmana, giver of wealth; I wish another favour for my devotee.
I do not wish for my devotee the earth full of jewels or a great heap of wealth; let him be righteous.
Let his mind delight in dharma and let him live by dharma; let him be chief in dharma; this I hold to be my favour."
[Manibhadra said:] "Since the kingdom and varied pleasures are the fruit of dharma, let him enjoy the fruits themselves, free of bodily affliction."
[Bhishma said:] Then Kundadhara of great fame did that very thing many times, practising dharma, and the deities were pleased with him.
[Manibhadra said:] "All those deities are pleased with him and with this brahmana; this righteous-souled one will set his mind on dharma."
[Bhishma said:] Then the cloud-bearer, Yudhishthira, his work done, having gained the wish of his mind, a boon hard for others to obtain,
saw then the fine garments of the best of the twice-born lying at his side, and came to despondency.
[The brahmana said:] "He does not know good deeds; who else will know what is done? I shall go to the forest; better to live by dharma."
[Bhishma said:] From despondency and the grace of the gods, that best of the twice-born entered the forest and began great austerity.
Living on roots and fruit, on the remains of offerings to gods and guests, the twice-born, great king, also came to delight in dharma.
Giving up all roots and fruit he became a leaf-eater; giving up leaves, the best of the twice-born then lived on water.
Later he lived on wind for many years, and his breath did not fail; it was as if a marvel.
To him, faithful in dharma and engaged in fierce austerity, after a great time divine vision arose.
The thought arose in him: "If, pleased, I were to give great wealth to someone, my word would not be false."
Then, with glad face, he took up austerity again and thought again what the perfected one attains above.
If, pleased, I were to give a kingdom to anyone, he would soon be king, and my word would not be false.
Kundadhara showed himself to him in person, Bharata, urged by friendship through the brahmana's austerity.
Meeting him, the brahmana honoured Kundadhara by rule, and was amazed, king.
Then Kundadhara said: "Your divine eye is the best; see the fate of kings, brahmana, and look at the worlds with that eye."
Then the brahmana saw from afar with the divine-joined eye thousands of kings sunk in hell.
[Kundadhara said:] "If, having honoured me with feeling, you should meet sorrow, what would I have done, and what would be the favour to you?
See, see again; how would a man wish for desires? For the door of heaven is shut, especially among men."
[Bhishma said:] Then he saw desire, anger, greed, fear, pride, sleep, drowsiness and sloth standing and covering men.
[Kundadhara said:] "By these the worlds are closed; the gods fear men, and by the gods' word they cause obstruction everywhere.
No one becomes righteous without the permission of the gods; you are able by austerity to give a kingdom and wealth."
[Bhishma said:] Then the brahmana fell with his head before the cloud-bearer and said, righteous-souled: "A great favour has been done to me.
That I envied you before through the bonds of desire and greed, not knowing your affection: forgive me for it."
Forgiven by me, said Kundadhara, and embracing the best of the twice-born in his arms, he vanished right there.
Then the brahmana roamed all these worlds, joined with austerity by the grace of Kundadhara, as before.
Travel through the sky, accomplishment of whatever he conceived, power from dharma, and the highest goal by yoga:
gods, brahmanas, the good, yakshas, men and charanas honour the righteous here, not the wealthy and not the desirous.
The gods are well pleased that your mind delights in dharma; in wealth there is a little part of happiness, but in dharma the highest happiness."
[Bhishma said:] "Here I shall relate to you what was told by Narada about the gleaner's sacrifice for a brahmana in former times.
In a realm of most excellent dharma, in the Vidarbhas, there was a twice-born, a gleaner, a certain sage, who performed sacrifice by sacrifice.
There his food was millet; the sun's wife Suvarchala, and bitter, tasteless greens, became sweet through austerity.
Approaching the earth in the forest, without harming any being, the sacrifice leading to heaven, scourge of foes, can be performed even with roots and fruit.
His wife, thin with vows, pure, wandering in the lotus-pond, was brought to be the sacrificer's wife; she is followed by truth, but, terrified of the curse, she did not follow her nature.
Her garment of the old leaves of the peacock-feathered leafy trees was made there, not by her wish, in the sacrifice, following the hotri.
By ill-thinking, the ignorant of dharma was born again from Shukra; in that forest near by a deer was a companion; it spoke truth in words: "A bad deed was done by you.
If this sacrifice becomes deformed, lacking in mantra and limbs, then, sir, throw me into the hotri's fire; go to heaven untiringly."
Thus addressed, she turned back and entered the sacrificial fire; desiring to see what bad conduct there was in the sacrifice, she went to the nether world.
With folded hands she begged the deer for truth again; embraced by truth, she was told, "Let it be gone."
Then the deer went eight steps and turned back: "Kill me well; killed by truth, I shall go to a good end.
See, with the eye I have given, the divine apsarases and the wondrous aerial cars of the great-souled gandharvas."
Then, seeing the lovely things with an eye clinging in longing, looking at the deer, she approved of heaven's dwelling by violence.
But Dharma, having become a deer, living many years in the forest, set up atonement for him; that was not the arrangement of sacrifice.
For him, by that feeling, with the mind of killing a deer then, great austerity was cut off; therefore violence is not for sacrifice.
Then the blessed Dharma himself had that sacrifice performed, and he gained by austerity the supreme concentration of his wife.
Non-violence is all of dharma; violence is not fitting in sacrifice; I shall tell you the truth, the dharma of truth-speakers."
[Bhishma said:] "You know all dharmas; you ask about the settled matter; hear liberation with disgust, sin and dharma from the root.
For the knowledge of the five, wish first arises; having attained them, desire or aversion is born, bull of the Bharatas.
Then he strives for it and undertakes action again, and wishes to practise the wished-for forms and scents.
Then attachment arises, and aversion after it; then greed arises, and delusion after it.
For one overcome by greed and delusion and joined with attachment and aversion, understanding does not arise in dharma, and he does dharma by pretext.
As he practises dharma by pretext, the pretext of wealth too pleases him, as wealth is gained by pretext, delight of the Kurus.
There he sets his mind, then wishes to do sin, though restrained by friends and by the learned, Bharata.
He gives a reply joined with reasoning and fitted by rule; his threefold adharma grows, born of attachment and delusion.
For him, by good conduct and practice, wisdom grows; he delights in dharma and lives by dharma.
Then he sets his mind on wealth gained by dharma, and waters the very root where he sees virtues.
So he becomes righteous-souled and gains a good friend; and by gain of friends and wealth he rejoices here and hereafter.
In sound, touch, form, taste and smell, Bharata, a creature gains mastery; this is known as the fruit of dharma.
Having gained the fruit of dharma he is not satisfied, Yudhishthira; unsatisfied, he takes up disgust with the eye of knowledge.
When the eye of wisdom sees only fault in desire, then he is detached from desires, and does not abandon dharma.
Seeing the world as perishable, he strives for total renunciation; then he strives for liberation, not by the wrong means but the right.
Slowly he takes up disgust and gives up sinful action; he becomes righteous-souled and gains the highest liberation.
This has been told you, dear, what you ask: sin, dharma, liberation and disgust, Bharata.
Therefore keep to dharma in every state, Yudhishthira; for those established in dharma, Kaunteya, perfection is eternal."
[Bhishma said:] "This is fitting in you, greatly wise, a skilful view, that you always seek all aims by means, sinless one.
The thought for making ghee is not for the birth of ghee, sinless one; so in the means to dharma there is no other cause in dharmas.
The road to the eastern sea does not go to the western; but the way to liberation is one; hear that at length from me.
One should cut off anger by forbearance, desire by giving up intentions; the steadfast should cut off sleep by cultivating goodness.
By heedfulness one should guard against fear, breath by practice of the knower of the field; wish, aversion and desire he should turn aside by steadiness.
Giddiness, delusion and whirling he should turn aside by practice; sleep and brilliance by the practice of knowledge, the knower of truth.
Troubles and diseases by moderate, wholesome, digestible diet; greed and delusion by contentment; objects by seeing the truth.
He should conquer adharma by compassion, dharma by disregard; hope by foresight, wealth by giving up attachment.
With sin shaken off, full of energy, light of diet, master of senses, having brought desire and anger under control, he should wish to lead himself to the seat of Brahman.
Freedom from delusion, from attachment, from desire and anger, from meanness, from overflow, from agitation, steadiness:
this is the path of liberation, serene, stainless, pure; so is restraint of speech, body and mind; otherwise it is by desire."
Knowing the aged Devala seated, Narada, best of the wise, asked about the origin and dissolution of beings.
Whence was this universe made, brahmana, moving and unmoving, and into what does it go at dissolution? Tell me that.
[Asita said:] "From which Time, urged by being, creates beings, the thinkers on beings say are the five great elements.
From them Time, urged by the self, creates beings; whoever speaks of anything beyond these speaks falsehood, without doubt.
Know, Narada, these five as eternal, unmoving and firm, heaps of great energy, with time as sixth, by nature.
Water, space, earth, wind and fire; beyond these elements, there is no success; doubt is gone.
Not by reasoning or logic would one speak falsehood, without doubt; you know them as come forth, whose heaps these are.
Those five, time, and being and non-being alone: the eight, the eternal elements of beings, their arising and passing.
First the creature perceives the objects separately by the senses; afterward it reflects by mind and then determines by intellect; he who determines all the things grasped by the senses.
Thought, the group of senses, mind, intellect, and the eighth: these are called the eight senses of knowledge by thinkers on the self.
Hands, feet, anus, genital and mouth as fifth: hear also these called the senses of action.
The mouth is called the sense for speech and eating; the feet the sense of movement; the hands for the instrument of action.
The anus and genital are the senses for discharge, similar in action, in the discharge of excrement and in the amorous discharge.
Strength resides in these, with speech rightly as taught; I have named all the qualities of knowledge, action and senses.
When the senses cease from their own actions through weariness, then with the withdrawal of the senses man sleeps.
If, with the senses stilled, the mind is not stilled and serves the objects, know it from the seeing of dreams.
The sattvic, rajasic and tamasic states: they praise those joined to action, the sattvic and the others.
Joy, success of actions, attainment, the highest goal: memory resorts to the states that are the causes of the sattvic.
In one of the creatures the states that follow the rule are ever sought of the two states, and the direct approach of both.
The senses and states are held to be seventeen qualities; the eighteenth is the embodied one, who is eternal in the body.
Or the qualities are all with bodies, resting in the embodied; when parted from that, they are bodiless and are not.
Or this is a combination, the body of five elements; these, ten and eight, are the qualities of the embodied; with heat the twentieth, a combination of five elements.
The great one supports this body with the wind; for it, joined with states, the cause is in the breaking of the body.
As anything arises and goes to its fivefold state, so at the end of the destruction of merit and demerit, driven by merit and demerit, he enters a body in time, then this one born of action.
Leaving and leaving, he goes from body to body, having taken refuge, driven by Time, the owner of the field, as from a broken house to a house.
There the wise of settled resolve do not grieve; but wretched men proud of their relations grieve.
He belongs to none, and none belongs to him; this one is alone ever, sharing pleasure and pain in the body.
The creature is never born, nor does he ever perish; having enjoyed the body, he goes sometime to the highest goal.
Wasting the body made of merit and demerit by the heap of action, the embodied one with spent body again attains Brahman-hood.
For the exhaustion of merit and demerit, Sankhya knowledge is ordained; at their exhaustion they see Brahman, the highest goal in the state of being."
[Yudhishthira said:] "This craving that arises from wealth: how, grandsire, shall we turn it back? For by craving we have been made to do sin."
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, sung by the king of Videha as he questioned Mandavya.
'I live very happily, for I have nothing at all; when Mithila is on fire, nothing of mine is burnt.
Riches, though abundant, are surely sorrow for those who know; and though not abundant, they ever bewilder the unwise.
The pleasure of desire in the world and the great divine pleasure do not equal a sixteenth part of the pleasure of the end of craving.
As the horn of a cow grows when she grows in due time, so craving grows as wealth grows.
When anything is conceived with the sense of mine, all of it becomes torment and, at its loss, arises again.
One should not follow desires; delight in desires is sorrow; having got wealth, one should use it, and avoid desire in dharma.
Having given up both truth and untruth, grief and joy, the dear and the undear, and having given up fear and fearlessness, one becomes perfectly calm and free of disease.
That craving, hard for the ill-minded to give up, which does not age as one ages, the disease that ends in death: happiness is for one who gives up that craving.
Seeing the conduct of the self, pure like the moon, free of disease, the righteous-souled gains fame, here and hereafter, happily.'
Hearing the king's words, the brahmana became glad; and honouring those words, Mandavya resorted to liberation."
[Bhishma said:] "Devoted to the dharmas of liberation, light of diet, master of senses, one reaches the highest place, which is beyond nature and firm.
Going forth from his house, equal in gain and loss, the sage should wander, without expectation of desires that rise.
He should not offend by eye, mind or speech; he should never speak a fault, directly or indirectly.
He should not harm any beings, and go the way of Maitrayana; having obtained this life, he should not make enmity with anyone.
He should bear harsh words, and never be proud; angered, he should speak kindly; abused, he should speak well.
He should not go in a circle clockwise or anticlockwise in the middle of the village; unless in need, he should not go for alms to a house previously marked.
Unscattered and well guarded, he should not speak unpleasantly; he should be gentle, not cruel in return, trusting, without anger.
Where there is no smoke, the pestle laid down, the embers gone, people having eaten, and the passing of vessels past, the sage should seek alms.
The ascetic should restrain the force of speech, of the mind, of anger, of contentiousness, of the belly and genitals; blame should not strike his heart.
He should stay neutral, equal toward praise and blame; this is the supreme purifier in the mendicant's stage.
Great-souled, of good vows, self-controlled, dependent on nothing anywhere, of unprecedented conduct, gentle, homeless, collected,
he should never mix with forest-dwellers and householders; he should seek unknown alms, and joy should not enter him.
For those who know, this is liberation; for those who do not, toil; this whole vehicle of liberation Harita spoke to the learned.
The twice-born who goes forth from the house, having given fearlessness to all beings, has radiant worlds and becomes fit for the endless."
[Yudhishthira said:] "The sorrow, best of the Kurus, that is met even by gods, when born as a human, honoured by the world, grandsire:
when shall we make renunciation, called sorrow? This bearing of bodies is sorrow, best of the Kurus.
Freed from the seventeen and the five causes, from the objects of the senses and the eight qualities, great-grandsire,
the sages of strict vows do not go to rebirth; when shall we be so, giving up the kingdom, scourge of foes?"
[Bhishma said:] "There is nothing endless, great king, all comes within reckoning; even rebirth is reckoned; nothing here is unmoving.
And one does not go, king; this fault is incidental; by effort alone, knower of dharma, you will go in time.
This embodied one is ever lord of merit and demerit, king; yet from them he is covered by the darkness that arises.
As a dusty wind, entering the crystal, is seen in its colour tinting the directions,
so the embodied one, tinted by the fruits of action and covered with darkness, colourless, turns in bodies relying on armour.
When a creature drives away by knowledge the darkness born of ignorance, then eternal Brahman would shine.
The sages say it is accomplished without effort; and those freed are to be served by you and the world with the gods; therefore the hosts of great sages are not at peace.
On this matter, long ago, hear what was sung, king, one-pointed, of how the Daitya Vritra acted when he had fallen from lordship.
Conquered, helpless, his kingdom taken, Bharata, not grieving among his enemies, relying on wisdom alone,
to Vritra fallen from lordship Ushanas formerly said: "Danava, have you no pain today, conquered?"
[Vritra said:] "By truth and austerity, knowing the destruction, I neither grieve nor rejoice at the coming and going of beings.
Beings urged by Time sink helpless in hell; the wise say all this has been seen to be divine.
Having spent the reckoned time urged by Time, with remaining time they are born again and again.
Having gone through thousands of animal wombs and even hell, helpless beings emerge, bound with the bonds of Time.
I have seen creatures so wandering; as the deed, so the gain: so the shastra shows.
Animal, hell, human and divine, having first practised pleasure, pain, the dear and the hated, all the world goes, joined with the ordinance of the end; and all beings go always the road gone.
[Bhishma said:] To him speaking, reckoned by the count of Time, whose resort is creation and maintenance, the blessed Ushanas answered: 'Dear, why do you speak these dreadful, wicked words?'
[Vritra said:] 'This is plain to you and other wise ones: the great austerity I performed long ago, greedy for victory.
Taking the scents and various juices of beings, I grew, striding over the three worlds by my own splendour.
Surrounded by garlands of flame, moving in the sky, I was unconquerable by all beings and ever fearless.
The lordship gained by austerity is lost by my own deeds; taking steadiness, blessed one, I therefore do not grieve.
When I wished to fight long ago with the great-souled Mahendra, I saw the blessed Hari Narayana, the lord.
Vaikuntha, Purusha, Vishnu, white, endless, eternal, with munja-grass hair and green beard, grandfather of all beings.
Surely a remainder of that austerity is still mine, since I wish to ask you, blessed one, the fruit of action.
In what class is great lordship founded, brahmana, and how does the highest lordship turn back?
By what do beings live or proceed again, or having attained what supreme fruit does the soul stay eternal?
By what action, or by what knowledge, brahmana sage, can that fruit be gained? You should explain that to me.'
Thus addressed, the sage then replied: 'Hear what I say, lion among kings, bull among men, with undivided mind together with your brothers.'"
[Sanatkumara said:] "He whose head and endless seat are, best of Danavas, of him I shall tell you the highest greatness, of Vishnu."
[Bhishma said:] While they spoke thus, the great sage Sanatkumara, righteous-souled, came to cut their doubt.
Honoured by the lord of the asuras and by the sage Ushanas, he sat on a seat, king, the bull among sages, most worthy.
To him seated, the greatly wise, Ushanas said: "Tell this lord of the Danavas the highest greatness of Vishnu."
Sanatkumara, hearing it, spoke to the wise lord of the Danavas words full of meaning, joined with the greatness of Vishnu.

Hear, Daitya, all this highest greatness of Vishnu; know, scourge of foes, that the whole world rests in Vishnu.
mahabharata:12:271.8	He creates the host of beings, moving and unmoving, mighty-armed; he draws them in at the time and again releases them; into him they go to dissolution and from him they arise.
mahabharata:12:271.9	He cannot be reached by Danava nature, nor by austerity or sacrifice, but only by restraint of the senses.
mahabharata:12:271.12	So the soul is purified in a hundred births by small action, and by great effort is purified in a single birth.
mahabharata:12:271.13	As one might wipe a little dust from one's body playfully, but removal of faults takes great effort.
There is no small bad deed of ours by which Agni was lost, or of yours, or mine; let this be examined in truth.
Unable to prevail, Indra, with bay horses, summoned Brihaspati and spoke these words together with the gods.
[Vaishampayana said:] Having said so to the king of dharma, trembling, with folded hands, King Dhritarashtra, son of Ambika, spoke these words.
Then, when Daruka had gone, Keshava, seeing Babhru near, said: "Guard the women; go quickly, so that robbers do not harm them from greed of wealth."
Even now human feeling touches you, lord of men; this is heaven; see the divine sages and perfected ones who dwell in the third heaven.
Today may the gods and gandharvas and the divine apsarases in heaven, stainless and sky-clad, attend you, auspicious one.
